topics.topic: Development of practical skills in biology

questions.prompt: Head circumference HC = 1.62 × (BPD + OFD). BPD = 76 ± 4.2 mm and OFD = 98 ± 6.5 mm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in HC. (1)
hints: Add absolute uncertainties when adding values.

questions.prompt: A length is 12.5 ± 0.5 mm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (1)
When two measurements are multiplied, how are their uncertainties combined? (1)
questions.solution: Add the percentage uncertainties [B1]

questions.prompt:
Potato slices in 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose had percentage mass changes of −8, −10, −12 and −10.

(i) Calculate the standard deviation using s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. (2)
(ii) Describe how to plot the mean with an error bar. (2)
(iii) Explain how sucrose concentration determines the change in mass. (3)
(iv) Suggest two factors in the method that could cause variation. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Deviations 2, 0, −2, 0; Σ = 8; 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67 [M1]
s = 1.63 [A1]
(ii) Plot the mean (−10) at 0.6 mol dm⁻³ [B1]
Error bar from −11.6 to −8.4 (± 1 SD) [B1]
(iii) Below the isotonic point, the solution has a higher water potential than the potato, so water enters — mass increases [B1]
Above it, water leaves by osmosis — mass decreases [B1]
The bigger the difference in water potential, the bigger the change [B1]
(iv) Slices not identical in size / not blotted consistently [B1]
Different times in solution / temperature variation / different potatoes [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to find the water potential of potato tissue. (9)
questions.solution:
Prepare sucrose solutions 0.0–1.0 mol dm⁻³ by dilution [B1]
Cut potato cylinders of equal size with a cork borer [B1]
Blot and weigh each [B1]
Place in solutions for a set time at constant temperature [B1]
Remove, blot, reweigh [B1]
Calculate percentage change in mass [B1]
Repeat at each concentration and calculate means [B1]
Plot percentage change against concentration [B1]
Find concentration with zero change; convert to water potential [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how error bars and standard deviations help interpret data from an osmosis experiment. (9)
questions.solution:
SD shows how spread out repeat values are around the mean [B1]
Small SD — data are precise / repeatable [B1]
Error bars plotted as mean ± 1 SD [B1]
About 68 % of values lie within ± 1 SD [B1]
If error bars of two means overlap, the difference may not be significant [B1]
If they don't overlap, the difference is likely to be significant [B1]
Large error bars suggest errors in method [B1]
Statistical test (t-test) gives a more reliable conclusion [B1]
Anomalies can be identified as values far from the mean [B1]

questions.prompt:
A peptide was heated with hydrochloric acid, then the products were separated by paper chromatography.

(i) Explain why the peptide was heated with acid, and why the paper should not be touched with fingers. (2)
(ii) A spot moved 4.6 cm and the solvent front moved 8.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Acid hydrolyses peptide bonds, releasing individual amino acids [B1]
Fingers would deposit amino acids / oils that would show up as extra spots [B1]
(ii) 4.6 ÷ 8.0 [M1]
= 0.58 [A1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to carry out paper chromatography of amino acids. (4)
questions.solution:
Draw a pencil origin line and spot the sample on it, drying between applications [B1]
Place in a solvent below the origin line in a sealed container [B1]
Remove before the solvent reaches the top; mark the solvent front [B1]
Spray with ninhydrin to show amino acids, then calculate Rf values [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why two-way chromatography may be needed to separate amino acids. (4)
questions.solution:
Some amino acids have similar Rf values in one solvent [B1]
So their spots overlap [B1]
The chromatogram is turned 90° and run in a second solvent [B1]
Amino acids with different solubilities in the second solvent separate [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give suitable axis labels for a line graph of cumulative percentage germination against time for each light colour. (2)
(ii) Evaluate a suggestion to weigh the dishes daily and calculate seed mass instead of counting germinated seeds. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) x-axis: time / hours [B1]
y-axis: cumulative germination / % [B1]
(ii) Mass gives quantitative data on growth [B1]
But mass changes with water uptake / evaporation, not just growth [B1]
Hard to separate seeds from damp paper; germination (radicle emergence) is what is being studied [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare fresh mass and dry mass as measures of plant growth. (5)
questions.solution:
Fresh mass is quick and doesn't kill the plant [B1]
But varies with water content, so unreliable [B1]
Dry mass: dry samples in an oven (e.g. 80 °C) until constant mass [B1]
More accurate measure of biomass [B1]
But plants are killed, so different plants must be used at each time [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how random errors and systematic errors affect results, and how each is reduced. (5)
questions.solution:
Random errors cause readings to vary unpredictably [B1]
Reduce precision; reduced by repeats and means [B1]
Systematic errors shift all readings in the same direction [B1]
Reduce accuracy; reduced by calibration / zeroing equipment [B1]
Repeats do not reduce systematic errors [B1]

questions.prompt:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on catalase using filter-paper discs soaked in enzyme dropped into hydrogen peroxide, timing how long each disc took to rise.

(i) Name the independent and dependent variables. (2)
(ii) Give two control variables. (2)
(iii) Explain how rate is calculated from the time. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Independent: temperature [B1]
Dependent: time for disc to rise [B1]
(ii) Concentration / volume of hydrogen peroxide [B1]
Size of disc / enzyme concentration / pH [B1]
(iii) Rate = 1 ÷ time [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would measure the initial rate of an enzyme reaction from a graph of product formed against time. (5)
questions.solution:
Plot product against time [B1]
Draw a tangent to the curve at time zero [B1]
Choose two points far apart on the tangent [B1]
Gradient = Δy ÷ Δx [B1]
Units, e.g. cm³ s⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to control temperature in an enzyme experiment and why pre-incubation matters. (5)
questions.solution:
Use a thermostatically controlled water bath [B1]
Check the temperature with a thermometer [B1]
Place enzyme and substrate in the bath separately first [B1]
So both reach the set temperature before mixing [B1]
Otherwise reaction starts at the wrong temperature [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the structures that generate movement in a sperm tail. (1)
questions.solution: Microtubules [B1]

questions.prompt: In which direction does DNA polymerase add nucleotides? (1)
questions.solution: 5′ to 3′ (adds to the 3′ end of the new strand) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why one strand is synthesised discontinuously during DNA replication. (1)
questions.solution: DNA polymerase only works 5′→3′, so on the antiparallel lagging strand DNA is made in short (Okazaki) fragments joined by ligase [B1]

questions.prompt: At ×600, the diameter of the field of view is 280 µm. Calculate its area to the nearest whole µm². (2)
Explain how to use a stage micrometer to calibrate an eyepiece graticule. (2)
questions.solution:
Line up the stage micrometer scale with the eyepiece graticule [B1]
Count divisions and calculate the length of one eyepiece unit (micrometer length ÷ eyepiece divisions); repeat for each objective [B1]

questions.prompt: 14 stomata were counted in a field of view of area 0.08 mm². Calculate the stomatal density per mm². (2)

(i) A leucocyte has a nucleus with three lobes and granular cytoplasm. Name it. (1)
(ii) Give two rules for an annotated biological drawing. (2)
(iii) Name the apparatus used to calibrate an eyepiece graticule. (1)
(iv) If 1 eyepiece unit = 2.5 µm and the cell measures 5 eyepiece units, calculate its diameter. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Neutrophil [B1]
(ii) Clear, continuous lines; no shading [B1]
Label lines ruled, not crossing; drawing large, in proportion [B1]
(iii) Stage micrometer [B1]
(iv) 5 × 2.5 [M1]
= 12.5 µm (13 µm to 2 s.f.) [A1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and function of neutrophils, lymphocytes and monocytes. (6)
questions.solution:
Neutrophils: lobed nucleus, granular cytoplasm [B1]
Phagocytose pathogens [B1]
Lymphocytes: large round nucleus, little cytoplasm [B1]
B and T cells — specific immunity [B1]
Monocytes: large, kidney-shaped nucleus [B1]
Develop into macrophages; present antigens [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why stains are used in light microscopy and give two examples. (6)
questions.solution:
Many cell structures are transparent [B1]
Stains increase contrast [B1]
Different stains bind to different structures [B1]
e.g. methylene blue stains nuclei / animal cells [B1]
e.g. iodine stains starch in plant cells [B1]
Differential staining (e.g. Gram stain) distinguishes cell types [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the phosphate group of a phospholipid as hydrophilic or hydrophobic, and explain why. (1)
questions.solution: Hydrophilic — it is charged / polar, so attracted to water [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of reaction that breaks down a phospholipid into its components. (1)
questions.solution: Hydrolysis [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the enzyme that hydrolyses triglycerides. (1)
questions.solution: Lipase [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond that joins nucleotides in a polynucleotide chain. (1)
questions.solution: Phosphodiester bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the two pyrimidine bases found in DNA. (1)
questions.solution: Cytosine and thymine [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why purines always pair with pyrimidines in DNA. (1)
questions.solution: Keeps the distance between strands constant (one double-ring + one single-ring base) and allows correct hydrogen bonding [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the bond that joins amino acids in a peptide. (1)
(ii) Name the reaction that forms it. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Peptide bond [B1]
(ii) Condensation [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the general structure of an amino acid. (2)
questions.solution:
Central carbon bonded to an amine group (NH₂) and a carboxyl group (COOH) [B1]
And a hydrogen atom and a variable R group [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why there are 20 different amino acids in proteins. (2)
questions.solution:
Each has a different R group [B1]
R groups differ in size, charge, polarity — allowing proteins to have many shapes and functions [B1]

questions.prompt:
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are enzymes with a zinc ion in the active site, a β-pleated sheet and three α-helices, and three histidine residues in the active site.

Match each feature to: primary structure, secondary structure, tertiary structure or cofactor. (3)
questions.solution:
Zn²⁺ in the active site — cofactor [B1]
β-pleated sheet and α-helices — secondary structure [B1]
Histidines in three places brought together in the active site — tertiary structure (positions in the sequence = primary) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a metal ion cofactor helps an enzyme work. (3)
questions.solution:
Ion binds to the enzyme, completing the active site shape [B1]
Helps substrate bind / forms enzyme–substrate complex [B1]
May take part in the reaction (e.g. stabilising charges) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the tertiary structure of an enzyme determines its specificity. (3)
questions.solution:
Folding produces a specifically shaped active site [B1]
Only substrates with a complementary shape can bind [B1]
Induced fit — active site moulds around the substrate [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how the drug marimastat could inhibit MMPs. (2)
questions.solution:
Has a similar shape to the substrate / binds to the active site (competitive inhibitor) [B1]
Binds the zinc ion, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form / less ECM protein hydrolysed [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare reversible and irreversible inhibitors. (2)
questions.solution:
Reversible inhibitors bind with weak bonds and can detach [B1]
Irreversible inhibitors bind with covalent bonds, permanently inactivating the enzyme [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain end-product inhibition. (2)
questions.solution:
The final product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an enzyme earlier in the pathway [B1]
So production slows when there is enough product (negative feedback) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of increasing temperature on enzyme activity from 10 °C to 70 °C. (4)
questions.solution:
Up to optimum, more kinetic energy [B1]
More collisions and enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Above optimum, bonds in tertiary structure break [B1]
Active site changes shape — enzyme denatured, rate falls [B1]

questions.prompt:
The rate of a reaction is 12 units at 20 °C and 21 units at 30 °C.

(i) Calculate Q10. (2)
(ii) Explain why Q10 is about 2 below the optimum. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 21 ÷ 12 [M1]
= 1.75 [A1]
(ii) A 10 °C rise roughly doubles the number of successful collisions [B1]
As molecules have more kinetic energy [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare competitive and non-competitive inhibitors. (4)
questions.solution:
Competitive inhibitors are similar in shape to the substrate and bind the active site [B1]
Their effect is reduced by increasing substrate concentration [B1]
Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere (allosteric site), changing the active site [B1]
Increasing substrate does not reverse it [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of facilitated diffusion in a living organism. (1)
questions.solution: Sodium ions entering a neurone through voltage-gated channels / glucose entering red blood cells via carriers [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of active transport in a living organism. (1)
questions.solution: Na⁺/K⁺ pump / mineral ion uptake by root hairs / sucrose loading into phloem [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of co-transport. (1)
questions.solution: Sodium–glucose co-transport in the ileum / proton–sucrose co-transport in companion cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the vessels where blood becomes oxygenated. (1)
questions.solution: Pulmonary capillaries (around the alveoli) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why regular exercise increases stroke volume. (1)
questions.solution: Ventricular hypertrophy — larger, stronger ventricles pump more blood per beat [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one change that stimulates the accelerator (sympathetic) nerve to the heart. (1)
questions.solution: Decrease in blood pH (increase in CO₂) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe the apoplast pathway by which substances move from root hair cells to the xylem. (2)
(ii) Describe and explain three adaptations of phloem sieve tubes for transporting sugars. (3)
(iii) Name the tissue in a vascular bundle that carries sucrose. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Through cell walls and spaces between cells, without crossing membranes [B1]
Blocked at the endodermis by the Casparian strip, so must enter the symplast [B1]
(ii) Sieve plates with pores allow flow between elements [B1]
Few organelles, so little resistance to flow [B1]
Companion cells with many mitochondria supply ATP for loading [B1]
(iii) Phloem [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem. (6)
questions.solution:
Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports sucrose and amino acids [B1]
Xylem vessels are dead; phloem sieve tubes are living [B1]
Xylem walls lignified; phloem walls cellulose [B1]
Xylem: no end walls; phloem: sieve plates [B1]
Xylem flow is one way (up); phloem flow is in both directions [B1]
Phloem has companion cells; xylem has pits [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe evidence for the mass flow hypothesis and one piece of evidence against it. (6)
questions.solution:
Aphid stylets inserted in phloem show sap is under pressure [B1]
Removing a ring of bark causes swelling above, as sugars accumulate [B1]
Radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ given to leaves appears in phloem and moves to sinks [B1]
Metabolic inhibitors stop translocation, showing active loading [B1]
Against: sugars move in different directions in the same tube / different rates for different solutes [B1]
Against: sieve plates would be expected to resist flow strongly [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe what VO₂ max means. (1)
(ii) Give one advantage of estimating VO₂ max from heart rates rather than measuring it directly. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) The maximum rate at which the body can take in and use oxygen during intense exercise [B1]
(ii) Quick / cheap / no specialist equipment / no need for exhausting exercise [B1]

questions.prompt: A student has a maximum heart rate of 200 bpm and a resting heart rate of 60 bpm. Calculate estimated VO₂ max using VO₂ max = 15 × (HRmax ÷ HRrest). (2)
Give two factors that affect a person's VO₂ max. (2)
questions.solution:
Fitness / training level / genetics [B1]
Age / sex / altitude / body mass [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why VO₂ max decreases immediately at high altitude, even though air still contains 21 % oxygen. (2)
(ii) Suggest why air temperature at altitude could affect VO₂ max. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Lower atmospheric pressure means lower partial pressure of oxygen [B1]
Smaller diffusion gradient into the blood / haemoglobin less saturated [B1]
(ii) Cold air may cause bronchoconstriction / more energy used for heat / affects enzymes [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the body acclimatises to high altitude over several weeks. (3)
questions.solution:
More EPO, so more red blood cells / haemoglobin [B1]
Increased ventilation rate [B1]
More capillaries / myoglobin / mitochondria [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people living at high altitude may have haemoglobin with a higher affinity for oxygen. (3)
questions.solution:
Partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is low [B1]
Higher affinity allows haemoglobin to become saturated in the lungs [B1]
Curve shifted to the left [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give two features of a relaxed sarcomere seen in an electron micrograph. (2)
(ii) Put these events in order: A: myosin heads bind to actin; B: Ca²⁺ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum; C: action potential reaches the muscle; D: tropomyosin moves; E: power stroke. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Long sarcomere / wide I band / visible H zone [B1]
Little overlap of actin and myosin [B1]
(ii) C, B, D, A, E [B2]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a sarcomere. (4)
questions.solution:
Section of myofibril between two Z lines [B1]
Thin actin filaments attached to Z lines [B1]
Thick myosin filaments in the middle (A band) [B1]
I band (actin only), H zone (myosin only), M line in the centre [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of calcium ions and ATP in muscle contraction. (4)
questions.solution:
Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, moving tropomyosin away from binding sites on actin [B1]
Myosin heads can bind, forming cross-bridges [B1]
ATP binding causes myosin heads to detach [B1]
ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the heads; ATP also pumps Ca²⁺ back into the SR [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the vessels that supply heart muscle with oxygen. (1)
(ii) Name the structures in the aortic arch and carotid arteries that detect pH. (1)
(iii) Name the vessel that carries blood from the right ventricle. (1)
(iv) Name the brain region containing the cardiovascular centre. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Coronary arteries [B1]
(ii) Chemoreceptors (aortic and carotid bodies) [B1]
(iii) Pulmonary artery [B1]
(iv) Medulla oblongata [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the route of blood through the heart from the vena cava to the aorta. (4)
questions.solution:
Vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle [B1]
Pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs [B1]
Pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle [B1]
Aortic valve → aorta [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the heart is described as a double pump. (4)
questions.solution:
Right side pumps blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation) [B1]
Left side pumps blood to the body (systemic circulation) [B1]
Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit [B1]
Allows high pressure to the body after low pressure in the lungs [B1]

questions.prompt:
A potometer showed a bubble moving 24 mm in 5 minutes. The capillary radius is 0.5 mm.

(i) Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. (3)
(ii) Explain why water uptake is not exactly equal to transpiration. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Volume = π × 0.5² × 24 [M1]
= 18.85 mm³ [M1]
÷ 5 = 3.8 mm³ min⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) Some water is used in photosynthesis [B1]
Some kept for turgor / cell growth [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how wind speed and humidity affect transpiration rate. (5)
questions.solution:
Water vapour diffuses out through stomata [B1]
Wind removes humid air near the leaf [B1]
Steeper water potential gradient, so faster transpiration [B1]
High humidity reduces the gradient [B1]
So transpiration slows [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to set up a potometer to give valid results. (5)
questions.solution:
Cut the shoot underwater [B1]
To prevent air entering xylem [B1]
Assemble apparatus underwater [B1]
Seal joints with petroleum jelly — airtight [B1]
Dry leaves; let shoot acclimatise before measuring [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how water moves up the xylem. (4)
questions.solution:
Water evaporates from leaves, lowering water potential [B1]
Creates tension pulling water up [B1]
Water molecules cohere by hydrogen bonds — continuous column [B1]
Adhesion to xylem walls; lignin prevents collapse [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe four adaptations of xerophytes to reduce water loss. (4)
questions.solution:
Thick waxy cuticle [B1]
Sunken stomata / hairs trap humid air [B1]
Rolled leaves [B1]
Reduced leaf area / spines [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure of xylem vessels and phloem sieve tubes. (4)
questions.solution:
Xylem: dead cells, no end walls [B1]
Lignified walls [B1]
Phloem: living sieve tube elements with sieve plates [B1]
Companion cells supply ATP; no lignin [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of a cereal grain that stores starch. (1)
questions.solution: Endosperm [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the layer of a barley grain that produces amylase when stimulated by gibberellin. (1)
questions.solution: Aleurone layer [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two conditions needed for seed germination. (1)
questions.solution: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature (any two) [B1]

questions.prompt: Of 115 cells observed, 20 were in prophase, metaphase, anaphase or telophase. Calculate the percentage in nuclear division. (1)
Name a tumour suppressor protein whose inactivation can lead to cancer. (1)
Give one feature of cells undergoing apoptosis. (1)
questions.solution: Cell shrinks / membrane blebbing / DNA fragmented / phosphatidylserine on outer membrane [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why meiosis is called a reduction division. (1)
(ii) Name an event in meiosis that can cause a chromosome mutation. (1)
(iii) Name a syndrome caused by a chromosome mutation. (1)
(iv) Suggest why cancers developing late in life are unlikely to be caused by errors in meiosis. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Chromosome number is halved, from diploid to haploid [B1]
(ii) Non-disjunction (or unequal crossing over / translocation) [B1]
(iii) Down's syndrome / Turner's / Klinefelter's [B1]
(iv) Meiotic errors would be in every cell from birth; late cancers arise from mutations in body cells during mitosis [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how non-disjunction causes Down's syndrome. (4)
questions.solution:
In meiosis, homologous chromosomes or chromatids of chromosome 21 fail to separate [B1]
One gamete gets two copies of chromosome 21 [B1]
Fertilisation with a normal gamete gives three copies (trisomy 21) [B1]
Risk increases with maternal age [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the main events of meiosis I. (4)
questions.solution:
Prophase I: homologous chromosomes pair up (bivalents) [B1]
Crossing over at chiasmata [B1]
Metaphase I: pairs line up randomly on the equator (independent assortment) [B1]
Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles, halving the chromosome number [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiotherapy as cancer treatments. (3)
questions.solution:
Chemotherapy: drugs kill dividing cells — affects healthy dividing cells too (hair loss, nausea) [B1]
Immunotherapy: e.g. monoclonal antibodies target cancer cells specifically / stimulate the immune system [B1]
Radiotherapy: ionising radiation damages DNA in tumour cells; some damage to nearby healthy tissue [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to target cancer cells. (3)
questions.solution:
Monoclonal antibodies are complementary to antigens found only on cancer cells [B1]
A drug / radioactive substance can be attached [B1]
So it is delivered directly to cancer cells, reducing harm to healthy cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why chemotherapy causes hair loss and lowers resistance to infection. (3)
questions.solution:
Chemotherapy drugs target rapidly dividing cells [B1]
Hair follicle cells divide rapidly, so are also damaged [B1]
Bone marrow cells are damaged, so fewer white blood cells [B1]

questions.prompt:
50 seeds were germinated under each of five light colours over 120 hours. In blue light, 24 % had germinated at 48 h and 70 % at 96 h. Germination was fastest in red light and slowest in far-red light.

(i) State two conclusions. (2)
(ii) Describe how to reduce random error. (2)
(iii) Calculate the percentage-point increase in blue light between 48 and 96 hours. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Germination is fastest / highest in red light [B1]
Far-red light inhibits germination / germination increases with time in all colours [B1]
(ii) Use more seeds / repeat with several dishes per colour [B1]
Calculate a mean / control temperature and water [B1]
(iii) 70 − 24 [M1]
= 46 percentage points [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why red light promotes germination and far-red light inhibits it in light-sensitive seeds. (6)
questions.solution:
Phytochrome exists as Pr and Pfr [B1]
Red light converts Pr to Pfr [B1]
Pfr is the active form, triggering germination [B1]
Pfr switches on genes for gibberellin synthesis [B1]
Far-red light converts Pfr back to Pr, inhibiting germination [B1]
Prevents germination under a leaf canopy, where light is rich in far-red [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens in a barley seed during germination. (6)
questions.solution:
Seed absorbs water (imbibition) [B1]
Embryo produces gibberellin [B1]
Gibberellin moves to the aleurone layer [B1]
Switches on genes for amylase [B1]
Amylase hydrolyses starch in the endosperm to maltose / glucose [B1]
Glucose used for respiration and growth of the embryo [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the process of sensitisation to an allergen. (1)
questions.solution: B cells produce IgE antibodies that bind to receptors on mast cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what happens when a sensitised person meets the allergen again. (1)
questions.solution: Allergen binds IgE on mast cells, causing release of histamine, which causes inflammation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antihistamines relieve allergy symptoms. (1)
questions.solution: They block histamine receptors, so histamine can't cause its effects [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a country of 260 million people, about 50 000 people died of AIDS in 1993. Deaths fell sharply after combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART) was introduced in 1996, to about 17 000 per year by 1998.

(i) Calculate the mortality rate per 100 000 in 1993. (2)
(ii) Discuss the effectiveness of HAART. (4)
questions.solution:
(i) 50 000 ÷ 260 000 000 × 100 000 [M1]
= 19 per 100 000 [A1]
(ii) Deaths fell by about two-thirds after HAART was introduced — suggests it is effective [B1]
HAART reduces viral replication, so T helper cells are preserved [B1]
But deaths may also have fallen due to education / safer sex / earlier diagnosis [B1]
HAART does not cure HIV — deaths levelled off rather than reaching zero; drug resistance / side effects [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how HIV leads to AIDS and how antiretroviral drugs slow this. (6)
questions.solution:
HIV infects T helper (CD4) cells [B1]
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from viral RNA, which integrates into host DNA [B1]
New viruses made and T helper cells destroyed [B1]
Falling T helper count weakens the immune system — opportunistic infections (AIDS) [B1]
Antiretrovirals inhibit reverse transcriptase / protease / integrase [B1]
Combination therapy reduces viral load and the chance of resistance [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between incidence and prevalence of a disease, and why prevalence of HIV can rise even when incidence falls. (6)
questions.solution:
Incidence is the number of new cases in a period [B1]
Prevalence is the total number of people with the disease at a time [B1]
Expressed per 100 000 population [B1]
With effective treatment, people with HIV live much longer [B1]
So fewer people leave the infected population through death [B1]
Prevalence rises even if fewer new infections occur [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ethical or social concerns for a person receiving a positive HIV test result. (2)
questions.solution:
Social stigma / discrimination at work [B1]
Difficulty getting insurance / mortgages; psychological stress; duty to inform partners [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two arguments for and against screening the population for a genetic disease with no cure. (2)
questions.solution:
For: allows people to plan / make reproductive decisions [B1]
Against: anxiety with no treatment available / risk of discrimination [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why patient confidentiality is important in testing for infectious diseases. (2)
questions.solution:
People are more likely to be tested and treated if results stay private [B1]
Protects people from discrimination / stigma [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why it has been difficult to develop an effective vaccine against HIV. (3)
questions.solution:
HIV mutates rapidly, changing its surface antigens (antigenic variability) [B1]
It infects and destroys T helper cells, which are needed for the immune response [B1]
It becomes latent / integrates into host DNA, hiding from the immune system [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how vaccination provides long-term immunity. (3)
questions.solution:
Vaccine contains antigens from a dead / weakened pathogen or purified antigen [B1]
Stimulates a primary immune response; B and T cells activated [B1]
Memory cells formed, giving a rapid secondary response on infection [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare prophylactic and therapeutic vaccines. (3)
questions.solution:
Prophylactic vaccines are given before infection to prevent disease [B1]
Therapeutic vaccines are given to people already infected to boost the immune response [B1]
e.g. HPV vaccine (prophylactic); experimental HIV / cancer vaccines (therapeutic) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give one advantage of a vaccine made from a purified protein rather than a live attenuated virus. (1)
(ii) In a trial, CD4 counts were compared over 48 weeks in two dose groups of a protein vaccine. Give two reasons why the vaccine's effectiveness can't be judged from these data. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Cannot cause the disease / cannot revert to a virulent form [B1]
(ii) No placebo / control group [B1]
Small sample / large variation / only one outcome measured / short time [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe three types of vaccine. (3)
questions.solution:
Live attenuated — weakened pathogen (e.g. MMR) [B1]
Inactivated / killed pathogen (e.g. flu injection) [B1]
Subunit / toxoid / mRNA vaccines containing only antigen or instructions for it [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a high percentage of a population must be vaccinated to control measles. (3)
questions.solution:
Measles is highly infectious — each case infects many others [B1]
About 95 % must be immune to break chains of transmission [B1]
Protecting those who can't be vaccinated (herd immunity) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give two consequences of a disease such as TB being notifiable. (2)
(ii) Name the type of antibiotic that kills bacteria by stopping cell wall synthesis. (1)
(iii) Outline how a population of Mycobacterium tuberculosis can become antibiotic resistant. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Cases are reported to public health authorities [B1]
Contacts traced and tested / outbreaks monitored / data on incidence collected [B1]
(ii) Bactericidal [B1]
(iii) Random mutation produces an allele for resistance [B1]
Antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survive (especially if treatment is not completed) [B1]
Resistant bacteria reproduce, so the resistant allele becomes more common [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how different antibiotics work, and why antibiotics don't affect human cells. (6)
questions.solution:
Penicillin inhibits enzymes that make peptidoglycan cross-links [B1]
Bacterial cell wall weakens and the cell bursts by osmosis (bactericidal) [B1]
Others (e.g. tetracycline) bind bacterial 70S ribosomes, stopping protein synthesis [B1]
Bacteriostatic — stop growth / reproduction [B1]
Human cells have no cell wall [B1]
Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, so are not affected [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why tuberculosis is treated with a combination of antibiotics over several months, and what DOTS involves. (6)
questions.solution:
TB bacteria grow slowly and can hide inside macrophages [B1]
Long treatment needed to kill all bacteria [B1]
Several antibiotics reduce the chance that a bacterium is resistant to all of them [B1]
Patients may stop early when they feel better, encouraging resistance [B1]
DOTS — directly observed treatment, short course [B1]
Health workers watch patients take their medication to ensure the course is completed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antimicrobial peptides (defensins) contribute to non-specific defence. (6)
questions.solution:
Defensins are produced by epithelial cells / neutrophils [B1]
They insert into and damage pathogen membranes, killing them [B1]
They aggregate pathogens, making them easier to engulf [B1]
They stimulate mast cells to release histamine, causing inflammation [B1]
They attract (chemotaxis) and activate phagocytes [B1]
Act against many pathogens — not specific, rapid [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the inflammatory response and explain how it helps fight infection. (6)
questions.solution:
Damaged cells and mast cells release histamine [B1]
Arterioles dilate — more blood to the area (redness, heat) [B1]
Capillaries become more permeable — plasma and proteins leave (swelling) [B1]
White blood cells move into the tissue [B1]
Phagocytes engulf pathogens [B1]
Higher temperature reduces pathogen reproduction [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Compare non-specific and specific immune responses. (6)
questions.solution:
Non-specific responds in the same way to all pathogens [B1]
Fast-acting — e.g. barriers, inflammation, phagocytosis [B1]
Specific response targets particular antigens [B1]
Involves lymphocytes (B and T cells) [B1]
Slower the first time [B1]
Produces memory cells, giving long-term immunity [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Daptomycin is an antibiotic with a hydrophilic core and a lipid tail that inserts into the cell membrane of Gram-positive bacteria.

(i) Suggest the type of molecule in the hydrophilic core. (1)
(ii) Explain how daptomycin could cause cytosol to leak from bacteria. (2)
(iii) Suggest why it may not work against Gram-negative bacteria. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Peptide / amino acids [B1]
(ii) Lipid tail inserts into the phospholipid bilayer [B1]
Forms pores / disrupts the membrane, so ions and cytosol leak out [B1]
(iii) Outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria prevents it reaching the cell membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics, with an example of each. (4)
questions.solution:
Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria [B1]
e.g. penicillin — weakens cell walls so bacteria lyse [B1]
Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria reproducing; immune system then removes them [B1]
e.g. tetracycline — inhibits protein synthesis at ribosomes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why new antibiotics are needed and why few have been developed recently. (4)
questions.solution:
Bacteria have evolved resistance to many existing antibiotics [B1]
Multidrug-resistant infections are increasingly hard to treat [B1]
Developing antibiotics is expensive and takes many years [B1]
Low profits — short courses / new antibiotics held in reserve [B1]

questions.prompt:
Bacteria are killed most effectively when the peak blood concentration (Cmax) of an antibiotic is at least 10 times the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). A patient's Cmax is 24 µg cm⁻³ and the MIC is 4 µg cm⁻³.

Comment on whether the dose is sufficient. (2)
questions.solution:
Cmax is only 6 times the MIC [B1]
Below the optimal ratio of 10, so the dose may not be sufficient / risk of resistance [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of an antibiotic. (2)
questions.solution:
The lowest concentration of the antibiotic [B1]
That prevents visible growth of the bacteria [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why low doses of antibiotics increase the risk of resistance developing. (2)
questions.solution:
Low doses kill the most susceptible bacteria but not partly resistant ones [B1]
Partly resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, selecting for resistance [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how vaccination provides long-term protection against a virus. (5)
questions.solution:
Vaccine contains antigens from the virus [B1]
Specific B cells / T cells are activated and clone [B1]
Plasma cells make antibodies [B1]
Memory cells remain [B1]
On infection, rapid secondary response destroys virus before symptoms [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain herd immunity and why a high vaccination rate is needed. (5)
questions.solution:
Enough people immune that the pathogen can't spread easily [B1]
Infected people are unlikely to meet susceptible people [B1]
Protects those who can't be vaccinated (infants, immunocompromised) [B1]
Required percentage depends on how infectious the disease is [B1]
e.g. about 95 % for measles [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a new influenza vaccine is needed each year. (5)
questions.solution:
Influenza virus mutates frequently [B1]
Changing the shape of its surface antigens (antigenic drift) [B1]
Memory cells / antibodies are no longer complementary [B1]
So no secondary response [B1]
Vaccine updated to match predicted strains [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of an antibody and relate it to its function. (4)
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains — two heavy, two light, held by disulfide bonds [B1]
Variable regions form antigen-binding sites complementary to one antigen [B1]
Constant region binds phagocyte receptors [B1]
Hinge region gives flexibility to bind two antigens — agglutination [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare active and passive immunity, with an example of each. (4)
questions.solution:
Active: own immune system makes antibodies; memory cells formed [B1]
e.g. vaccination / infection [B1]
Passive: antibodies given; no memory cells, short-lived but immediate [B1]
e.g. antibodies across placenta / in breast milk / antivenom [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Helper T cells bind antigen presented by APCs [B1]
Release cytokines activating B cells and cytotoxic T cells [B1]
Cytotoxic T cells bind infected cells presenting antigen [B1]
Release perforin, killing the infected cell [B1]

questions.prompt: State the net gain of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule. (1)
How many triose phosphate molecules are needed to make two glucose molecules? (1)
Name the product of glycolysis that enters the link reaction. (1)
questions.solution: Pyruvate [B1]

questions.prompt: Where is ATP synthase found in a chloroplast? (1)
questions.solution: Thylakoid membranes [B1]

questions.prompt: A pigment moved 7.0 cm and the solvent front moved 7.5 cm. Calculate the Rf value. (1)
Explain what a high Rf value tells you about a pigment. (1)
questions.solution: It is very soluble in the solvent / less attracted to the paper, so travels further [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons, other than regenerating ATP and glycogen, why extra oxygen is needed after exercise. (2)
questions.solution:
To oxidise lactate back to pyruvate / glucose in the liver [B1]
To re-oxygenate myoglobin and haemoglobin / support raised metabolic rate and body temperature [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why lactate is produced during intense exercise. (2)
questions.solution:
Oxygen demand exceeds supply, so oxidative phosphorylation can't keep up [B1]
Pyruvate is reduced to lactate, regenerating NAD so glycolysis can continue [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why breathing rate stays high after exercise has stopped. (2)
questions.solution:
To repay the oxygen debt — extra oxygen used to break down lactate [B1]
CO₂ levels are still high, stimulating chemoreceptors [B1]

questions.prompt: In Calvin's experiment with algae and radioactive CO₂, give a reason for each step: (i) illuminating the algae for 30 minutes first; (ii) placing heat-absorbing glass between lamps and flask; (iii) running samples into hot alcohol. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) So photosynthesis reaches a steady rate before CO₂ is added [B1]
(ii) Prevents heating, so temperature stays constant [B1]
(iii) Kills cells / denatures enzymes, stopping reactions instantly [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how radioactive tracers can be used to study metabolic pathways. (3)
questions.solution:
A substrate is labelled with a radioactive isotope (e.g. ¹⁴C) [B1]
Samples taken at intervals and compounds separated (chromatography) [B1]
Order in which compounds become radioactive shows the sequence of reactions [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why Calvin used a thin, flat vessel ("lollipop") for algae. (3)
questions.solution:
Large surface area to volume ratio [B1]
All algae receive similar light [B1]
Quick sampling through a tap at the bottom [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the enzyme that first fixes CO₂ into an organic molecule. (1)
(ii) After 2 s most radioactivity was in GP; after 10 s in triose phosphate; after 30 s in hexose sugars. Explain the order. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) RuBisCO [B1]
(ii) CO₂ combines with RuBP to form GP first [B1]
GP is reduced to TP using ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
TP then combines to form hexoses / regenerates RuBP [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the three stages of the Calvin cycle. (4)
questions.solution:
Carbon fixation: CO₂ + RuBP → 2 GP, catalysed by RuBisCO [B1]
Reduction: GP reduced to TP using reduced NADP and ATP [B1]
Regeneration: most TP converted back to RuBP using ATP [B1]
Remaining TP used to make glucose, amino acids, lipids [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why RuBisCO is described as inefficient, and how this affects photosynthesis at high temperatures. (4)
questions.solution:
RuBisCO works slowly [B1]
It can also bind oxygen instead of CO₂ [B1]
Photorespiration wastes energy and releases CO₂ [B1]
Increases at high temperature / low CO₂, reducing net photosynthesis [B1]

questions.prompt: Calvin initially thought a 2-carbon compound was the first product of CO₂ fixation. Explain why this was wrong. (2)
questions.solution:
The first product was GP, a 3-carbon compound [B1]
CO₂ combines with 5-carbon RuBP, forming an unstable 6C compound that splits into two 3C GP molecules [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how scientific theories change over time. (2)
questions.solution:
New evidence from better techniques / experiments may not fit an existing theory [B1]
Theory is modified or replaced after peer review and repeated experiments [B1]

questions.prompt: Predict what happens to the concentration of RuBP if the CO₂ supply to an illuminated plant is suddenly cut off. (2)
questions.solution:
RuBP rises [B1]
Not used to fix CO₂, but still regenerated from TP [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A leaf of area 0.97 m² had a maximum CO₂ uptake of 25 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum CO₂ uptake in 1 minute. (2)
(ii) Explain the significance of the point where net photosynthesis is zero. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) 25 × 0.97 × 60 [M1]
= 1455 µmol [A1]
(ii) Compensation point — rate of photosynthesis equals rate of respiration [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why net photosynthesis is negative in the dark. (3)
questions.solution:
No light, so no photosynthesis [B1]
Respiration continues [B1]
So CO₂ is released (net uptake negative) [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant's net CO₂ uptake is 18 units in light, and its CO₂ release in the dark is 4 units. Calculate gross photosynthesis and explain. (3)
questions.solution:
Gross = 18 + 4 [M1]
= 22 units [A1]
Assumes respiration rate is the same in light and dark [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why oxygen is needed for germination. (2)
(ii) Suggest how germinating seeds take up oxygen from the soil. (1)
(iii) Suggest why seedlings take in less oxygen from the soil once leaves appear. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) For aerobic respiration [B1]
To produce ATP for growth / cell division / enzyme synthesis [B1]
(ii) Diffusion through the seed coat / root surface from air spaces in the soil [B1]
(iii) Leaves photosynthesise, producing oxygen [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why germinating seeds release heat and lose dry mass at first. (4)
questions.solution:
Stored food (starch / lipids) is respired [B1]
Some energy released as heat [B1]
CO₂ is lost, so dry mass decreases [B1]
No photosynthesis until leaves form, so no new organic matter [B1]

questions.prompt: Seeds rich in oil have an RQ of about 0.7 when germinating; starchy seeds have an RQ of about 1.0. Explain. (4)
questions.solution:
RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ used [B1]
Oily seeds respire lipids [B1]
Lipids have less oxygen per carbon, so need more O₂ — RQ about 0.7 [B1]
Starchy seeds respire carbohydrate — equal CO₂ and O₂, RQ = 1.0 [B1]

questions.prompt:
During intense exercise, muscle pH falls.

(i) Explain why lactate builds up in muscle during intense exercise. (2)
(ii) Explain how a fall in pH reduces enzyme activity in muscle. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Oxygen supply is insufficient for aerobic respiration [B1]
Pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD so glycolysis continues [B1]
(ii) H⁺ ions interact with charged R groups, breaking ionic / hydrogen bonds [B1]
Active site changes shape, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not [B1]
Aerobic produces about 30–32 ATP per glucose; anaerobic only 2 [B1]
Aerobic products are CO₂ and water; anaerobic product is lactate [B1]
Anaerobic occurs only in the cytoplasm; aerobic also in mitochondria [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why breathing rate stays high after intense exercise has stopped. (4)
questions.solution:
Extra oxygen is needed to repay the oxygen debt [B1]
Lactate is converted back to pyruvate [B1]
Pyruvate is oxidised aerobically or converted to glucose in the liver [B1]
Oxygen also needed to restore myoglobin oxygen and ATP / creatine phosphate stores [B1]

questions.prompt:
Athletes took sodium bicarbonate before a 400 m race. Mean race time fell from 52.4 s to 51.9 s.

(i) Calculate the percentage decrease in race time. (2)
(ii) Suggest how sodium bicarbonate could improve performance. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 0.5 ÷ 52.4 × 100 [M1]
= 0.95 % [A1]
(ii) Bicarbonate acts as a buffer, removing H⁺ ions [B1]
So pH falls less and enzymes / muscle contraction continue for longer [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the combined contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy. (1)
questions.solution: Oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH and LH secretion, so no follicles mature / no ovulation [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the hormone that triggers ovulation. (1)
questions.solution: Luteinising hormone (LH) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the structure that secretes progesterone after ovulation. (1)
questions.solution: Corpus luteum [B1]

questions.prompt:
A mutation in a gene for a sperm-coating protein reduces sperm's ability to penetrate cervical mucus. In one population, 22 % of men are homozygous for the mutation.

(i) Suggest why the mutation may reduce the chance of fertilisation. (2)
(ii) Calculate the frequency of the mutant allele to 2 significant figures. (2)
(iii) Suggest why the allele remains common. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Fewer sperm pass through cervical mucus [B1]
So fewer reach the oviduct / egg; sperm may be destroyed by the immune system [B1]
(ii) q = √0.22 [M1]
= 0.47 [A1]
(iii) Homozygous men still father children (fertility reduced, not zero) / heterozygotes unaffected / possible heterozygote advantage [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe IVF and ICSI as treatments for infertility. (5)
questions.solution:
IVF: hormones stimulate several eggs to mature [B1]
Eggs collected and mixed with sperm in a dish [B1]
Embryos develop for a few days, then 1–2 are transferred to the uterus [B1]
ICSI: a single sperm is injected directly into an egg [B1]
Used when sperm can't penetrate the egg / low sperm count [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe spermatogenesis. (5)
questions.solution:
Takes place in the seminiferous tubules of the testes [B1]
Spermatogonia (diploid) divide by mitosis [B1]
Some grow into primary spermatocytes, which undergo meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes [B1]
Meiosis II produces haploid spermatids [B1]
Spermatids differentiate into spermatozoa, nourished by Sertoli cells [B1]

questions.prompt:
Studies show that drinking alcohol during pregnancy is linked to lower birth mass and learning difficulties, though some studies found no clear effect of light drinking. Health advice is to avoid alcohol completely when pregnant or trying to conceive.

Evaluate this advice. (6)
questions.solution:
Alcohol crosses the placenta into fetal blood [B1]
Fetal liver can't break it down well [B1]
Can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorder — damage to brain development, low birth mass [B1]
Early weeks are critical for organ development, often before a woman knows she is pregnant [B1]
Some studies show no clear effect of low intake, but no safe level has been proven [B1]
Advice is precautionary and simple to follow — justified [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the placenta is adapted for exchange between mother and fetus, and why some harmful substances can cross it. (6)
questions.solution:
Chorionic villi give a large surface area [B1]
Thin barrier between maternal and fetal blood — short diffusion distance [B1]
Countercurrent-like flow / maternal blood in spaces maintains concentration gradients [B1]
Oxygen, glucose, amino acids, antibodies cross to the fetus; CO₂ and urea cross back [B1]
Small or lipid-soluble substances (alcohol, nicotine, drugs) diffuse across [B1]
Some viruses (e.g. rubella) can cross [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how smoking during pregnancy can affect the fetus. (6)
questions.solution:
Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carried [B1]
Less oxygen reaches the fetus [B1]
Nicotine constricts blood vessels, reducing placental blood flow [B1]
Less glucose and nutrients reach the fetus [B1]
Low birth mass / premature birth [B1]
Increased risk of miscarriage / stillbirth [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
(i) Give one adaptation of maize flowers for wind pollination. (1)
(ii) Describe the events after a pollen grain lands on the stigma that lead to formation of the embryo and endosperm. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Large feathery stigmas / anthers hang outside / lots of light pollen [B1]
(ii) Pollen tube grows down the style, controlled by the tube nucleus [B1]
Enters the ovule through the micropyle [B1]
One male nucleus fuses with the egg (zygote → embryo); the other fuses with the polar nuclei (triploid endosperm) [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the features of wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers. (4)
questions.solution:
Insect-pollinated: large, brightly coloured petals, scent, nectar [B1]
Insect-pollinated: sticky / spiky pollen, stigmas inside the flower [B1]
Wind-pollinated: small / no petals, no scent or nectar [B1]
Wind-pollinated: lots of light, smooth pollen; feathery stigmas and anthers outside the flower [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to the ovule and ovary after fertilisation in flowering plants. (4)
questions.solution:
Zygote develops into the embryo [B1]
Endosperm forms the food store [B1]
Integuments become the seed coat (testa); ovule becomes the seed [B1]
Ovary becomes the fruit [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name one hormone that increases and one that decreases in concentration at the menopause. (2)
(ii) Give one factor, other than ageing, that can cause menopause. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Increases: FSH / LH [B1]
Decreases: oestrogen / progesterone [B1]
(ii) Removal of ovaries / chemotherapy / radiotherapy [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why FSH levels rise at the menopause. (3)
questions.solution:
Ovaries run out of follicles [B1]
Less oestrogen and inhibin produced [B1]
Less negative feedback on the pituitary, so more FSH is released [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three effects of the menopause on the body. (3)
questions.solution:
Hot flushes / night sweats [B1]
Reduced bone density — osteoporosis [B1]
Increased risk of cardiovascular disease / mood changes [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain how benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) prevents the bladder emptying completely. (2)
(ii) Give one other change to the male reproductive system with ageing. (1)
(iii) Suggest why there is no national screening programme for prostate cancer in the UK. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Prostate enlarges and presses on the urethra [B1]
Narrowing it, so urine flow is reduced [B1]
(ii) Lower testosterone / lower sperm count / erectile dysfunction [B1]
(iii) The PSA test is unreliable — false positives and false negatives [B1]
May lead to unnecessary treatment of slow-growing cancers with side effects [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the criteria a disease should meet before a national screening programme is introduced. (5)
questions.solution:
The condition is an important health problem [B1]
There is a detectable early stage [B1]
A reliable, safe and acceptable test exists [B1]
Effective treatment is available for early cases [B1]
Benefits outweigh harms and costs [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of testosterone in males. (5)
questions.solution:
Development of male sex organs before birth [B1]
Secondary sexual characteristics at puberty [B1]
e.g. deepening voice, facial hair, muscle growth [B1]
Stimulates sperm production [B1]
Made by interstitial (Leydig) cells under LH control [B1]

questions.prompt: A forest has a GPP of 18 000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and plant respiration of 6 500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. Calculate NPP. (1)
questions.solution: 11 500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt: Define net primary productivity. (1)
questions.solution: The rate at which energy is stored as biomass in producers after respiratory losses (GPP − R) [B1]

questions.prompt: What range of values can Σ(n/N)² take in Simpson's index? (1)
questions.solution: Between 0 and 1 (D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² also ranges 0–1) [B1]

questions.prompt:
The demographic transition model shows how birth and death rates change as a country develops (Stages 1–5).

(i) Describe how population size changes through the stages. (2)
(ii) Suggest why birth rates fall between Stages 2 and 3. (3)
(iii) Suggest why birth rate may fall below death rate in Stage 5. (1)
hints: Gap between birth and death rate.
questions.solution:
(i) Stable and low in Stage 1; increases rapidly in Stages 2–3 as death rate falls [B1]
Levels off in Stage 4; may decline slightly in Stage 5 [B1]
(ii) Access to contraception / family planning [B1]
Women's education and employment; lower infant mortality so fewer children needed [B1]
Urbanisation — children cost more and contribute less to family income [B1]
(iii) Ageing population / people having children later or not at all / high cost of raising children [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the death rate falls in Stage 2 of the demographic transition, and the consequences for population structure. (6)
questions.solution:
Improved sanitation and clean water reduce infectious disease [B1]
Better food supply / nutrition [B1]
Vaccines and medicines reduce deaths, especially of children [B1]
Birth rate remains high, so population grows rapidly [B1]
Population pyramid has a wide base — many young people [B1]
Later, ageing population gives a narrower base and wider top [B1]

questions.prompt:
A country has a birth rate of 32 per 1000 and a death rate of 12 per 1000 per year, and a population of 15 million.

(i) Calculate the natural increase per year. (2)
(ii) Estimate the population after 1 year. (2)
(iii) Give two factors, other than birth and death rates, that affect population size. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 20 per 1000 = 2 % [M1]
0.02 × 15 million = 300 000 per year [A1]
(ii) 15 000 000 + 300 000 [M1]

In 2019, 19.3 % of people in low- and middle-income countries were food insecure. A target is to reduce this to 9.2 % by 2029.

Pests evolve resistance [B1]

questions.prompt:
Divers placed a tape-measure grid over a 100 m² area of coral reef and randomly selected five 1 m² areas to survey.

Capture a sample using traps, mark them harmlessly and release [B1]
Leave time for marked animals to mix with the population [B1]
Capture a second sample and count marked animals [B1]
Population = (first sample × second sample) ÷ number marked in second [B1]

40 woodlice were caught and marked. Later, 50 were caught, of which 8 were marked.

Percentage cover of seven species on a reef: 30, 25, 15, 10, 10, 5, 5.

Corals can't tolerate low salinity / sediment blocks light, so sensitive species die [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how rising sea temperatures and ocean acidification threaten coral reef biodiversity. (4)
questions.solution:
Higher temperatures cause corals to expel symbiotic algae (bleaching) [B1]
Corals lose their food source and may die [B1]
CO₂ dissolves in seawater, lowering pH [B1]
Calcium carbonate skeletons dissolve / grow more slowly, so reef habitats are lost [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why coral reefs have very high biodiversity. (4)
questions.solution:
Complex 3D structure provides many habitats / niches [B1]
Warm, sunny, shallow water — high productivity [B1]
Symbiotic algae provide energy at the base of the food web [B1]
Many food sources support many species [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a karyotype is prepared from cells in metaphase. (1)
questions.solution: Chromosomes are fully condensed and visible, so can be counted and arranged [B1]

questions.prompt: What would a karyotype show for a person with Turner's syndrome? (1)
questions.solution: 45 chromosomes, with only one X chromosome (XO) [B1]

questions.prompt: Two heterozygous parents for cystic fibrosis have a child. What is the probability the child has cystic fibrosis? (1)

(i) Explain what is meant by a palindromic DNA sequence. (1)
(ii) Name a type of bacterial endonuclease other than Cas9. (1)

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between sticky ends and blunt ends, and why sticky ends are useful. (3)
questions.solution:
Sticky ends are produced by a staggered cut, leaving short single-stranded overhangs [B1]
Blunt ends are produced by a straight cut [B1]
Sticky ends can pair with complementary ends from other DNA cut with the same enzyme, making joining easier [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare Cas9 with restriction enzymes. (3)
questions.solution:
Both are bacterial nucleases that cut DNA [B1]
Restriction enzymes recognise a fixed short sequence [B1]
Cas9 is guided by a programmable guide RNA, so can cut almost any sequence [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of CRISPR and RNA interference (RNAi) for studying gene function. (4)
questions.solution:
CRISPR permanently knocks out a gene by editing DNA [B1]
RNAi temporarily silences a gene by destroying its mRNA — reversible / partial knockdown [B1]
CRISPR may have off-target cuts; knocking out essential genes may be lethal [B1]
RNAi may not completely silence the gene / off-target effects [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how RNA interference silences a gene. (4)
questions.solution:
Double-stranded RNA is cut into short siRNA [B1]
siRNA joins a protein complex (RISC) [B1]
Single strand pairs with complementary mRNA [B1]
mRNA is cut / blocked, so not translated [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the ethical issues of using CRISPR to edit human embryos. (4)
questions.solution:
Could prevent serious inherited diseases [B1]
Changes are inherited by future generations — long-term effects unknown [B1]
Off-target mutations could cause harm [B1]
Concerns about designer babies / consent of future people [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the coding and non-coding regions of a pre-mRNA molecule, and the process that produces mature mRNA. (3)
questions.solution:
Coding regions: exons [B1]
Non-coding regions: introns [B1]
Splicing removes introns and joins exons [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how one gene can code for several different proteins. (3)
questions.solution:
Pre-mRNA contains several exons [B1]
Exons can be spliced together in different combinations [B1]
Producing different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how DNA methylation and histone acetylation control gene expression. (3)
questions.solution:
Methylation of cytosine prevents transcription factor binding, silencing genes [B1]
Histone acetylation loosens chromatin, allowing transcription [B1]
Deacetylation condenses chromatin, preventing transcription [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Define the terms gene and allele. (2)
(ii) Iceland was settled by a small number of people, and its population later fell sharply because of plagues and a volcanic eruption. Name the effect of each event on allele frequencies. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Gene: a sequence of DNA bases coding for a polypeptide / functional RNA [B1]
Allele: an alternative form of a gene [B1]
(ii) Small number of settlers: founder effect [B1]
Population crash: genetic bottleneck [B1]

questions.prompt: Define genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous. (4)
questions.solution:
Genotype: the alleles an organism has [B1]
Phenotype: observable characteristics, from genotype and environment [B1]
Homozygous: two identical alleles of a gene [B1]
Heterozygous: two different alleles of a gene [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how genetic drift can change allele frequencies in a small population. (4)
questions.solution:
Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequency [B1]
In small populations, chance determines which individuals reproduce [B1]
Alleles may be lost or become fixed regardless of advantage [B1]
Reduces genetic diversity [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a founder effect and a population bottleneck lead to low genetic diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
Only a small number of individuals reproduce, carrying a small proportion of the alleles of the original population [B1]
Many alleles are lost by chance; population regrows from few individuals, so diversity stays low [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a genetically homogeneous population is useful for genetic research into disease. (2)
hints: Easier to link alleles to disease.
questions.solution:
Less genetic variation, so fewer confounding genetic factors [B1]
Easier to identify alleles linked to a disease; good genealogical records help [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why genetic disorders are more common in isolated populations. (2)
questions.solution:
People are more likely to share recessive alleles from common ancestors [B1]
So more children inherit two copies and show the disorder [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how flow cytometry could be used to study blood cells in people at risk of a blood cancer. (4)
questions.solution:
Blood cells are labelled with fluorescent antibodies specific to surface proteins [B1]
Cells pass one at a time through a laser beam [B1]
Detectors measure fluorescence and light scattering of each cell [B1]
Numbers of each cell type counted rapidly / abnormal cells detected [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how genome-wide association studies identify alleles linked to disease. (4)
questions.solution:
DNA from many people with and without the disease is analysed [B1]
Many SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) across the genome are compared [B1]
SNPs more common in patients are associated with the disease [B1]
Large samples needed; association doesn't prove causation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how advances in DNA sequencing have improved understanding of disease. (4)
questions.solution:
High-throughput sequencing makes sequencing whole genomes fast and cheap [B1]
Genomes of many people can be compared to find disease-linked mutations [B1]
Pathogen genomes sequenced to track outbreaks / develop vaccines [B1]
Allows personalised medicine [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a single gene mutation causes sickle cell anaemia. (3)
questions.solution:
A substitution in the β-globin gene changes one codon, replacing glutamic acid with valine [B1]
Haemoglobin molecules stick together at low oxygen, forming fibres [B1]
Red blood cells become sickle-shaped, carry less oxygen and block capillaries [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the sickle cell allele is common in areas where malaria is widespread. (3)
questions.solution:
Heterozygous people (sickle cell trait) are more resistant to malaria [B1]
So they survive and reproduce more than homozygous normal people [B1]
Passing on the allele — balanced polymorphism [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why sickle cell anaemia shows codominance. (3)
questions.solution:
Heterozygotes produce both normal and sickle haemoglobin [B1]
Both alleles are expressed [B1]
Heterozygotes have mild symptoms (sickle cell trait) — intermediate phenotype [B1]

questions.prompt: For each feature, state whether it occurs in transcription only, translation only, both or neither: (i) C pairs with G; (ii) A pairs with T; (iii) phosphodiester bonds form; (iv) peptide bonds form. (4)
questions.solution:
(i) Both [B1]

(iii) Transcription only [B1]
(iv) Translation only [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare transcription and translation. (4)
questions.solution:
Transcription occurs in the nucleus; translation on ribosomes in the cytoplasm [B1]
Transcription uses DNA as a template; translation uses mRNA [B1]
Transcription uses RNA polymerase; translation uses ribosomes and tRNA [B1]
Transcription makes mRNA; translation makes a polypeptide [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and role of tRNA. (4)
questions.solution:
Single strand folded into a clover-leaf shape by hydrogen bonds [B1]
Has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon [B1]
Binds a specific amino acid at the 3′ end [B1]
Brings amino acids to the ribosome in the correct order [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why red–green colour blindness mostly affects males. (2)
questions.solution:
The allele is recessive and on the X chromosome [B1]
Males have only one X, so one recessive allele causes the condition; females need two [B1]

questions.prompt: A carrier woman has children with a man who has normal colour vision. What is the probability that a son will be colour blind? (2)
questions.solution:
Sons receive Xᴮ or Xᵇ from mother, Y from father [M1]
Probability = 0.5 [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a colour-blind father cannot pass the condition to his sons. (2)
questions.solution:
Fathers pass their Y chromosome to sons [B1]
The allele is on the X chromosome, which goes only to daughters [B1]

questions.prompt:
In maize, smooth (A) is dominant to wrinkled (a) and yellow (B) is dominant to colourless (b). F1 smooth yellow plants (AaBb) were test-crossed with wrinkled colourless plants.

1 smooth yellow : 1 smooth colourless : 1 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled colourless [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by epistasis, using an example. (4)
questions.solution:
Epistasis is when one gene affects / masks the expression of another gene [B1]

If homozygous recessive (cc), no pigment — albino, whatever the other gene [B1]

questions.prompt: Two AaBb plants are crossed. Calculate the expected numbers of each phenotype from 320 offspring. (4)

A test cross gave 152 smooth yellow, 148 wrinkled colourless, 48 smooth colourless and 52 wrinkled yellow (400 total). Expected numbers were 100 each.

(iii) Suggest an explanation. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) (52² + 48² + 52² + 48²) ÷ 100 [M1]
= (2704 + 2304 + 2704 + 2304) ÷ 100 [M1]
χ² = 100.2 [A1]
(ii) Much greater than 7.82, so reject the null hypothesis — significant difference from 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 [B1]

Parental combinations most common; recombinants only from crossing over [B1]

100 ÷ 400 × 100 [M1]
= 25 % [A1]

About 25 map units apart [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the steps in using a χ² test to compare observed and expected results of a genetic cross. (6)
questions.solution:
State a null hypothesis (no difference between observed and expected) [B1]
Calculate expected numbers from the predicted ratio [B1]
Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E [B1]
Degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1 [B1]
Compare with the critical value at p = 0.05 [B1]
If χ² is greater, reject the null hypothesis; if less, accept it [B1]

A cross was expected to give a 3 : 1 ratio. 160 offspring were 128 dominant and 32 recessive.

questions.prompt: Explain how a single base substitution may or may not affect a protein. (4)

questions.prompt: Explain how abscisic acid causes stomata to close. (2)

Water potential rises, so water leaves by osmosis; guard cells become flaccid and close the pore [B1]

questions.solution:
H⁺ pumped out; K⁺ enters guard cells, lowering water potential [B1]
Water enters by osmosis, guard cells become turgid and the thicker inner walls bend apart [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the endocrine structures in the pancreas that secrete insulin and glucagon. (1)
(ii) Discuss the mechanisms that keep blood glucose at 80–90 mg per 100 cm³, naming the cells and biochemical pathways involved. (6)
hints: α and β cells; glycogenesis etc.

(ii) β cells detect high glucose and secrete insulin [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how glucagon raises blood glucose using a second messenger. (7)

Activates a G protein [B1]
Activates adenylyl cyclase [B1]

cAMP activates protein kinase A [B1]

Brain cells rely almost entirely on glucose [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe a glucose tolerance test and how results differ in a person with diabetes. (3)
questions.solution:

Blood glucose measured at intervals for 2 hours [B1]
In diabetes, glucose rises higher and takes much longer to return to normal [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why type 2 diabetes is often treated with diet and exercise first, rather than insulin. (3)

Weight loss and exercise increase insulin sensitivity of cells [B1]
Reducing sugar intake prevents large rises in blood glucose [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why winter wheat seeds given a cold treatment can flower when sown in spring. (2)

Long-day plants flower when Pfr is high; short-day plants when Pfr is low [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how growers can make chrysanthemums flower at any time of year. (5)

Chrysanthemums are short-day (long-night) plants [B1]
Covering plants with black-out sheets lengthens the night [B1]
Low Pfr induces flowering [B1]
Night-break lighting prevents flowering until required [B1]
So flowering can be timed for the market [B1]

questions.prompt:

Blurred / cloudy vision, faded colours [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of the cornea, lens, iris, retina, fovea and optic nerve. (6)

Cornea — refracts light [B1]
Lens — fine focusing [B1]
Iris — controls pupil size / amount of light entering [B1]
Retina — contains photoreceptors [B1]
Fovea — high density of cones, sharp colour vision [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why age-related macular degeneration affects central vision and the ability to read. (6)
questions.solution:
The macula is the central part of the retina [B1]

questions.prompt:

(ii) Describe what happens in a rod cell at rest (dark) and in light. (2)

questions.prompt: Describe the role of rhodopsin in the response of a rod cell to light. (3)

questions.prompt: Give three examples of sensory receptors and the energy each converts. (3)
questions.solution:
Rods / cones — light [B1]
Pacinian corpuscles — pressure / mechanical [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the actions of the vagus nerve, the sympathetic (accelerator) nerve and adrenaline in controlling heart rate. (6)
questions.solution:
