Increases heart rate and force of contraction [B1]
Adrenaline is a hormone carried in the blood, increasing heart rate and stroke volume [B1]
Nerves act quickly and briefly; adrenaline is slower but longer lasting and widespread [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how heart rate is adjusted during exercise. (6)
questions.solution:
Muscles respire faster, producing more CO₂, lowering blood pH [B1]
Chemoreceptors detect the fall in pH [B1]
Stretch receptors in muscles detect movement [B1]
Impulses to the cardiovascular centre in the medulla [B1]
More impulses along the sympathetic nerve to the SAN [B1]
Heart rate increases; adrenaline also released [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and functions of the autonomic nervous system. (6)
questions.solution:
Part of the peripheral nervous system controlling involuntary activities [B1]
Two divisions — sympathetic and parasympathetic [B1]
Sympathetic: prepares for activity (fight or flight), noradrenaline [B1]
Parasympathetic: rest and digest, acetylcholine [B1]
Often antagonistic — e.g. heart rate, pupil size [B1]
Motor pathways have two neurones with a ganglion between [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the clotting cascade, naming the enzyme released by platelets, the soluble protein converted to an insoluble one, and the ion required. (4)
questions.solution:
Damaged tissue and activated platelets release thromboplastin [B1]
Thromboplastin converts prothrombin to thrombin, with calcium ions [B1]
Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin [B1]
Fibrin mesh traps red blood cells and platelets, forming a clot [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how anticoagulants such as warfarin and heparin reduce the risk of thrombosis. (4)
questions.solution:
Warfarin blocks the action of vitamin K needed to make clotting factors [B1]
So fewer clotting factors are made [B1]
Heparin inhibits thrombin / activates antithrombin [B1]
So fibrin is not formed, reducing clot formation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with haemophilia bleed for longer, and why it is more common in males. (4)
questions.solution:
Faulty allele means a clotting factor (VIII) isn't made [B1]
Cascade can't proceed, so less fibrin forms [B1]
The allele is recessive and on the X chromosome [B1]
Males have one X, so one faulty allele causes the condition [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using plasma to replace blood lost during childbirth. (2)
(ii) Give one other use of donated plasma. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Advantage: no need for blood group matching / contains clotting factors / restores volume [B1]
Disadvantage: contains no red blood cells, so doesn't restore oxygen-carrying capacity [B1]
(ii) Extraction of clotting factors / antibodies / albumin for burns patients [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a person with blood group A cannot receive blood from a group B donor. (3)
questions.solution:
Group B red cells carry B antigens [B1]
Group A plasma contains anti-B antibodies [B1]
Antibodies bind the antigens, causing agglutination / clotting [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why donated blood is stored with citrate and kept cool. (3)
questions.solution:
Citrate binds calcium ions, preventing clotting [B1]
Cool temperature slows cell metabolism / respiration [B1]
And slows bacterial growth [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how blood glucose concentration is lowered after a meal. (5)
questions.solution:
Rise detected by β cells in the islets of Langerhans [B1]
Insulin secreted into the blood [B1]
Binds receptors on liver / muscle cells [B1]
More glucose channels (GLUT4) in membranes, so more uptake [B1]
Glucose converted to glycogen (glycogenesis) and respired [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how blood glucose is raised during fasting. (5)
questions.solution:
Fall detected by α cells [B1]
Glucagon secreted [B1]
Binds liver cell receptors; activates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP [B1]
Activates enzymes for glycogenolysis [B1]
And gluconeogenesis from amino acids / glycerol [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes in cause and treatment. (5)
questions.solution:
Type 1: β cells destroyed (autoimmune), no insulin [B1]
Treated with insulin injections [B1]
Type 2: cells less responsive to insulin / less insulin produced [B1]
Linked to obesity, age, inactivity [B1]
Treated with diet, exercise, then drugs (e.g. metformin) / insulin [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why control of blood glucose is an example of negative feedback. (3)
questions.solution:
A change from the set point is detected [B1]
Response reverses the change [B1]
Returns glucose towards normal, then response stops [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of positive feedback in the body and explain why it is not homeostatic. (3)
questions.solution:
e.g. oxytocin in childbirth / depolarisation of neurones [B1]
Change causes further change in the same direction [B1]
Moves away from, not back to, a set point [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a blood glucose biosensor works. (3)
questions.solution:
Contains immobilised glucose oxidase [B1]
Enzyme oxidises glucose [B1]
Produces a current proportional to glucose concentration [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the nephron produces urine. (6)
questions.solution:
High pressure in glomerulus forces small molecules into Bowman's capsule [B1]
Basement membrane acts as filter; proteins and cells stay in blood [B1]
Glucose reabsorbed in the PCT by co-transport with Na⁺ [B1]
Loop of Henle creates low water potential in the medulla [B1]
Water reabsorbed from collecting duct by osmosis [B1]
Controlled by ADH [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the body responds to dehydration. (6)
questions.solution:
Blood water potential falls [B1]
Detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus [B1]
More ADH released from posterior pituitary [B1]
ADH binds collecting duct cells [B1]
More aquaporins inserted into membranes [B1]
More water reabsorbed — small volume of concentrated urine [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how cells of the proximal convoluted tubule are adapted for reabsorption. (6)
questions.solution:
Microvilli give a large surface area [B1]
Many mitochondria provide ATP [B1]
For active transport of Na⁺ out into the blood [B1]
Creating a gradient for co-transport of glucose / amino acids [B1]
Close to capillaries — short diffusion distance [B1]
Water follows by osmosis [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how haemodialysis removes urea but keeps glucose in the blood. (4)
questions.solution:
Blood flows past a partially permeable membrane against dialysis fluid [B1]
Dialysis fluid has no urea, so urea diffuses out [B1]
Fluid contains glucose at normal blood concentration [B1]
So no net glucose diffusion; countercurrent keeps gradients [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare dialysis and kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure. (4)
questions.solution:
Dialysis: frequent sessions, diet restrictions [B1]
Available without waiting for a donor [B1]
Transplant: normal life and diet, cheaper long term [B1]
But shortage of donors, surgery risk and lifelong immunosuppressants [B1]

questions.prompt: Give causes of kidney failure and explain the effects on the body. (4)
questions.solution:
Causes: diabetes / high blood pressure / infection [B1]
Urea and waste build up in blood [B1]
Fluid builds up — oedema, high blood pressure [B1]
Ion imbalance (e.g. K⁺) affects heart rhythm [B1]

questions.prompt: Brain volume and β-amyloid levels were measured in 50 patients. Name the test for a correlation between them. (1)
questions.solution: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the test used to compare the means of two measurements taken from the same individuals before and after treatment. (1)
questions.solution: Paired t-test [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one pathological change seen in the brain of a person with Alzheimer's disease. (1)
questions.solution: β-amyloid plaques between neurones / neurofibrillary tangles of tau inside neurones / loss of neurones [B1]

questions.prompt: As soil water content fell over 6 days, ABA in leaves rose and stomatal opening fell. Discuss whether these data show that dry soil promotes ABA synthesis, causing stomata to close. (3)
questions.solution:
Data show a correlation between drying soil, more ABA and stomatal closure [B1]
But correlation doesn't prove causation / where ABA was made isn't shown [B1]
Other factors may change (e.g. leaf water potential); need experiments adding ABA / sample size [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to test whether ABA causes stomatal closure. (3)
questions.solution:
Apply ABA solution to leaves of well-watered plants; apply water to controls [B1]
Measure stomatal aperture (nail varnish peels) or water loss after a set time [B1]
Control other variables; repeat with several plants and compare statistically [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a correlation and a causal relationship. (3)
questions.solution:
A correlation is a relationship where two variables change together [B1]
A causal relationship means a change in one directly causes the change in the other [B1]
Causation needs a controlled experiment / known mechanism; a third factor may cause both [B1]

questions.prompt: Outline a method to investigate the effect of a fitness training programme on the estimated VO₂ max of school students. (6)
questions.solution:
Measure resting and maximum heart rate (e.g. after a bleep test) before the programme [B1]
Calculate estimated VO₂ max [B1]
One group follows the training programme for several weeks; a control group does not [B1]
Groups matched for age, sex, initial fitness; large sample [B1]
Repeat measurements at the end under the same conditions [B1]
Compare change using a paired / unpaired t-test; ethical considerations (consent, health) [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain the physiological changes that increase VO₂ max with endurance training. (6)
questions.solution:
Cardiac muscle enlarges — greater stroke volume and cardiac output [B1]
Lower resting heart rate [B1]
More capillaries in muscles [B1]
More mitochondria and myoglobin in muscle fibres [B1]
Increased blood volume / red blood cells [B1]
Stronger respiratory muscles / better ventilation [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Discuss the ethical issues of carrying out exercise investigations on school students. (6)
questions.solution:
Informed consent needed — parental consent for under-16s [B1]
Right to withdraw at any time [B1]
Health screening — exclude students with heart or asthma conditions [B1]
Risk of injury / overexertion — supervision needed [B1]
Confidentiality of data [B1]
Avoid pressure on students; activities appropriate for age [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Evaluate studying a large group of people with an early-stage condition to see who progresses to cancer, compared with studying family pedigrees. (4)
questions.solution:
Large group: more data, can identify environmental and genetic risk factors statistically [B1]
But takes many years / expensive / loss of participants [B1]
Pedigree analysis shows inheritance patterns within families [B1]
But small numbers; shared environment confounds; can't separate genes and environment easily [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare cohort studies and case-control studies. (4)
questions.solution:
Cohort: follows a group over time to see who develops the disease [B1]
Good for showing risk factors, but slow and expensive [B1]
Case-control: compares people with the disease to matched people without, looking back at exposures [B1]
Quicker, good for rare diseases, but relies on memory / records — bias [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a pedigree can show whether a condition is caused by a dominant or recessive allele. (4)
questions.solution:
Recessive: can skip generations [B1]
Two unaffected parents can have an affected child [B1]
Dominant: every affected person has at least one affected parent [B1]
Two affected parents can have an unaffected child [B1]

questions.prompt:
MMP activity was much higher in grade III (most severe) breast tumours than in other grades (p < 0.0001).

(i) State a null hypothesis. (1)
(ii) Use "probability" and "chance" to state the conclusion. (1)
(iii) Evaluate the hypothesis that MMP activity increases cancer severity. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) There is no difference in MMP activity between grade III tumours and other tumours [B1]
(ii) The probability that the difference is due to chance is less than 0.01 %, so reject the null hypothesis [B1]
(iii) Supports a link — higher MMP in more severe tumours [B1]
But correlation; severe tumours might produce more MMP rather than MMP causing severity [B1]
Sample size / variation within grades not known; mechanism plausible (MMPs break down ECM, allowing spread) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what p < 0.05 means and why biologists use 0.05 as the significance level. (5)
questions.solution:
p is the probability that the results are due to chance [B1]
p < 0.05 means less than 5 % probability that the difference is due to chance [B1]
So the null hypothesis is rejected and the result is significant [B1]
0.05 balances the risk of wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis [B1]
Against missing a real effect [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how tumours spread to other parts of the body (metastasis), and why MMPs might be involved. (5)
questions.solution:
Malignant cells detach from the primary tumour [B1]
MMPs digest the extracellular matrix and basement membrane [B1]
Cells invade surrounding tissue and enter blood / lymph vessels [B1]
Carried to other organs, forming secondary tumours [B1]
Inhibiting MMPs could slow spread [B1]

questions.prompt:
150 women using HRT and 150 not using HRT rated their perceived risk of breast cancer and uterine cancer from 1 to 10. Both groups rated breast cancer risk higher than uterine cancer risk, and HRT users rated both risks lower than non-users.

Draw conclusions and suggest reasons for the differences. (4)
questions.solution:
Both groups perceive breast cancer as a greater risk than uterine cancer [B1]
HRT users perceive lower risks than non-users [B1]
Users may have been informed by doctors / chose HRT because they think risks are low [B1]
Perceived risk is subjective — may not reflect actual risk; non-users may avoid HRT due to fears [B1]

questions.prompt: Give advantages and disadvantages of using questionnaires in health research. (4)
questions.solution:
Cheap and quick to collect data from many people [B1]
Can collect information about opinions and lifestyle [B1]
Responses may be dishonest / affected by memory [B1]
Self-selection bias; questions may be leading [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the benefits and risks of hormone replacement therapy. (4)
questions.solution:
Benefit: relieves menopausal symptoms (hot flushes) [B1]
Benefit: reduces osteoporosis risk [B1]
Risk: slightly increased risk of breast cancer [B1]
Risk: increased risk of blood clots / stroke [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a trial of sodium bicarbonate on athletic performance should be designed so its results are valid. (4)
questions.solution:
Use a placebo (e.g. salt solution) for comparison [B1]
Double blind so neither athletes nor researchers know who had which [B1]
Crossover design — same athletes test both, in random order [B1]
Large sample; control diet, rest and conditions [B1]

questions.prompt: Mean 400 m times with bicarbonate and placebo differed by 0.5 s, but the standard deviations were about 1.2 s. Evaluate the claim that bicarbonate improves performance. (4)
questions.solution:
Bicarbonate gave a faster mean time [B1]
But SDs are large relative to the difference — data overlap [B1]
The difference may not be significant [B1]
A statistical test (e.g. paired t-test) is needed; small samples reduce confidence [B1]
